2.text: badly treated may leave of his own accord, and will seek his luck elsewhere.

3.text: In poor families such cases are very frequent. Young men leave their parents’

4.text: homes displeased with the poverty and bad luck of the domestic hearth, and

5.text: travel for many hundred miles to seek positions with well-to-do reindeer-owners.

6.text: Even a girl may leave her father’s house, if the family want to force a mar-

7.text: riage entirely against her inclinations. Of course, such incidents are rare.

8.text: Still I know of two cases of flight which were carried out with success. Both

9.text: took place in summer, when pursuit over long distances is very difficult. In

10.text: one case, the girl returned to her former husband, from whom she had been

11.text: taken by her family, in accordance with Chukchee custom. In the other case,

12.text: the girl married into a new family; and her father, after some quarrelling,

14.text: Among the Maritime Chukchee, whoever wants to leave his family may

15.text: go to another house and become an adopted son-in-law, or he may go away to

16.text: the Reindeer people and get a position with the owner of a large herd.

17.text: Violent quarrels between father and sons may lead even to murder. I

18.text: mentioned¹ a case of parricide which happened near Cape Erri in the family

19.text: of a rich reindeer-owner, and in which the wife, the son, and the nephew of

20.text: the one killed took part. Old Cossack reports mention similar cases. Thus

21.text: the Anadyr Cossack Boris Kusnetzky, who was captured by the Chukchee in

22.text: 1754, mentions in his report of 1763 to Lieut.-Col. Plenisner, chief officer of

23.text: Okhotsk, that while in captivity he witnessed a son stab his father with a

24.text: knife and a brother stab his brother out of mere spite.²

25.text: ADOPTION. — A married couple who have no children may adopt some

26.text: little child, most frequently a boy, the son of some related family, like that

27.text: of a brother or a cousin; but the child may also belong to an unrelated friend

28.text: or simply to a “neighbor in the camp.” Such a child becomes in the house

30.text: bor is poor and has many children, and the foster father is rich in reindeer,

31.text: the child is given away with much pleasure. The foster father, moreover,

32.text: gives to the real father a “joyful present,” consisting of a couple of live rein-

33.text: deer, mostly those suitable for driving. The ceremonial of adoption is similar

34.text: to that of marriage. A reindeer is slaughtered as a sacrifice to the Morning

35.text: Dawn; and the adopted child, together with his foster parents, is anointed

36.text: with blood. The marks of the new family are used in anointing, which sym-

37.text: bolizes that the child joins the new hearth, with its special charms and “luck

38.text: in life.”³ Notwithstanding this, with a boy of foreign descent, the ties of
